title: Wine Wimsey Review · Mon Nov 2 (round 2)
subtitle: Round 2: 6 approved kept (posts #3, 8, 9, 15 and stories 1, 3). 14 rejected slots replaced from the inbox (13 typed quotes + 2 images, oldest first), plus 1 extra post (#17) so all 15 inbox items are used. Feed is 17 (15 images + 1 TOBI at #6 + the extra), stories 4. Flags: #13 uses The Settled One per Scott's inbox note; #12 and #16 are both daylight-saving 6:30 jokes (both from the inbox); #11 keeps the typed 'One:' prefix and the story with the clocks quote keeps its stray closing quote mark, word for word

posts.quote: Nothing gets you ready for the day you look in the mirror and realize your younger self packed up and left without saying goodbye.
posts.caption: I found my first grey streak in 2011 and gave it a name. It has since been joined by the whole committee, and the mirror no longer pretends to be surprised.
posts.first: There's a photo of me from college on the fridge that I walk past every morning. I look at it the way you look at a house you used to rent. Friendly, curious, no wish to move back in. The light in that kitchen was excellent, though.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun leaning toward a bathroom mirror with a hand on her cheek and a wistful squint, a wine glass beside the sink. Text in the speech bubble reads: Nothing gets you ready for the day you look in the mirror and realize your younger self packed up and left without saying goodbye.

posts.quote: Me 30 years ago, 9:00 PM, Ready to turn heads. Me now, 9:00 PM, Ready to turn over.
posts.caption: The 9 p.m. version of me used to start with a hairbrush and a plan. Now it starts with a heating pad and a very specific pillow arrangement. The cat on my left foot has been staring at the ceiling fan for forty minutes like he's reconsidering something. By 9:04 the lamp is off and the day is handed over to whoever runs the dark. Nobody has complained. The best part of the evening is how nobody asks for anything.
posts.first: I got up at 2 a.m. for water and found all four cats exactly where I'd left them, arranged like a very soft puzzle. I got back in on the one corner they'd left me. Eleven minutes later, I was out cold again. Nobody has ever slept better or taken up less room.
posts.alt: Two-panel cartoon comic. Top panel, labeled Me 30 years ago, 9:00 PM: a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun applies lipstick at a glowing vanity mirror. Caption: Ready to turn heads. Bottom panel, labeled Me now, 9:00 PM: she sleeps in bed with her mouth open, surrounded by four sleeping cats. Caption: Ready to turn over.

posts.quote: The website asked me to prove I'm not a robot by picking every square with a bus. I'd like to speak to whoever decided what counts as a bus.
posts.caption: Four rounds. The corner of a bus counted in round two and did not count in round four, and no one has explained why to me.
posts.first: I got it on the fifth try, with the motorcycle I'd skipped. I felt no triumph. The computer said welcome and I said, thanks, I guess, and closed the lid very gently. Next time I'm picking the traffic lights.
posts.alt: Comic-panel cartoon of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun squinting suspiciously at a laptop at a kitchen table, a wine glass in her hand. Text at the top reads: The website asked me to prove I'm not a robot by picking every square with a bus. I'd like to speak to whoever decided what counts as a bus.

posts.quote: I’m sure my patience is around here somewhere. It’s probably off hiding with my memory and my metabolism.
posts.caption: The patience went first, I think, though I couldn't swear to it. I noticed at the post office, somewhere between window two and the sign asking me to take a number. That was about three years ago, and I keep expecting it to turn up like a library book. I've checked the car and both coats. My memory left a note on the fridge that says back soon, which is how I know it's gone for good too. The metabolism sent a postcard.
posts.first: Last week I found a gift card from 2019 in a coat pocket, still good. It felt like the universe handing me a small refund. I'm hoping the patience is in a different coat. I plan to check them all by Friday.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun on her hands and knees looking under a sofa cushion with a flashlight, a wine glass on the coffee table. Text in the speech bubble reads: I’m sure my patience is around here somewhere. It’s probably off hiding with my memory and my metabolism.

posts.quote: When I was a kid, making ashtrays for our parents counted as a sweet school craft. Nothing says childhood like homemade smoking supplies.
posts.caption: The clay one was my best work, and it was about the size of a dinner roll. My mother kept it by the kitchen sink for years, which I now understand was an act of love.
posts.first: We made them in third grade out of clay that dried gray and cracked on one side. I painted mine green because the green paint was closest. My dad kept paper clips in it until it got lost in a garage move. I still think about that green.
posts.alt: Comic-panel cartoon of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding up a lumpy green clay dish with a wry look at a kitchen table, a shelf of crooked childhood crafts behind her and a wine glass on the table. Text at the top reads: When I was a kid, making ashtrays for our parents counted as a sweet school craft. Nothing says childhood like homemade smoking supplies.

posts.quote: After standing here for a few minutes, I’ve decided whatever I came in this room for can come find me.
posts.first: I walked into the spare room at 2:40 and stood in the middle of it for a full minute. The room was patient. I eventually left with a roll of tape I didn't know I needed, which felt like a fair trade. Whatever I came for is probably still in there, waiting.

posts.quote: I thought I’d grown out of my teenage attitude. Then menopause brought it back, with sharper comebacks and nobody left to ground me.
posts.caption: At fifteen my mother grounded me for a week over what she called my tone. I'm now fifty-two and the tone has come back with better material and a hand fan. There's nobody left to take my phone away, and it turns out the phone was never the point. The comebacks are faster and drier now, and mostly aimed at the thermostat. The thermostat has not responded. I take that as agreement.
posts.first: My mother called last Sunday and asked why I sounded short. I said I was fine, with a little extra on the fine. There was a pause on the line. Then she said now you know, and hung up very pleased with herself.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sitting sideways in an armchair with her arms crossed, rolling her eyes and holding a folding fan, a wine glass on the side table. Text in the speech bubble reads: I thought I’d grown out of my teenage attitude. Then menopause brought it back, with sharper comebacks and nobody left to ground me.

posts.quote: I hit reply all today. Sixty people now know what I think of the potluck sign-up sheet.
posts.caption: I had a point. It was a fair one about the six bags of chips already signed up. But I made it in the wrong place at 2:15, with a tone I'd planned to delete. Someone replied with a thumbs-up, which I've decided to read as solidarity. The silence afterward was the loudest part. I sat there refreshing the inbox like the email might come back on its own. It didn't. I closed the laptop, took a walk around the block, and came home to eleven new messages, ten of them about chips.
posts.first: I brought a pie to the potluck anyway. Nobody mentioned the email. Three people told me the pie was good, in the careful voice you use around a thing that might go off. It was a good pie. I mention it because it was.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at a cluttered desk staring in horror at a laptop with her hands on her cheeks, a coffee mug and wine glass beside it. Text in the speech bubble reads: I hit reply all today. Sixty people now know what I think of the potluck sign-up sheet.

posts.quote: First frost this morning. I stood on the porch in my robe and scraped the windshield with a spatula. It worked. Don't ask.
posts.caption: The scraper lives in the garage, which was a different zip code at 7:05. The spatula was on the counter, and it's flat, and it was right there. It does a better job than the real scraper and I am not looking into why. The pancakes will taste the same. I washed it first. The neighbor across the road has an actual ice scraper with a glove attached and I will say nothing against it. Mine is in the garage somewhere and the spatula was right there. The kitchen smelled like cold air and burnt toast for an hour afterward.
posts.first: The robe was my husband's idea in 2011. It has since outlived two coats and an opinion. I wore it on the porch and the neighbor waved. I waved back with the spatula. The spatula is back in the drawer. It has never looked prouder.
posts.alt: Painted illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun in a flannel robe scraping frost from a station wagon windshield with a metal spatula on a farmhouse porch at sunrise. Text at the top reads: First frost this morning. I stood on the porch in my robe and scraped the windshield with a spatula. It worked. Don't ask.

posts.quote: The radio just called one of my favorite ’80s songs an “oldie.” That kind of disrespect was completely uncalled for.
posts.caption: It was Tuesday and I was making toast, and the DJ said it so casually. The toast went cold. So did something else.
posts.first: I told my nephew about it at dinner and he said that song is forty years old. I said I'm aware of the number and the song is fine, thank you. He went back to his plate. Some things people have to work out on their own.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at a kitchen counter with a hand on her chest looking offended, a retro radio and a wine glass beside her, cassette tapes on a shelf. Text in the speech bubble reads: The radio just called one of my favorite ’80s songs an “oldie.” That kind of disrespect was completely uncalled for.

posts.quote: One: I used to be young, wild, and totally carefree. Now I catch myself saying, “I should probably head out before it gets dark.”
posts.caption: There was a time the evening started at ten and ended when the sun came up. Now I'm in bed with the lamp on by 9:15 and I count that as a late night. Nobody warned me the switch would be this gentle. One day you're closing the place down, and the next you're annoyed at how dark the driveway is. I keep a flashlight by the door now and I'm not embarrassed. It has very good batteries, which is more than I can say for my knees.
posts.first: I drove home at dusk last Friday and turned the high beams on twice just to be safe. A deer looked at me, I looked at the deer, and we agreed on a speed. I got home at 5:50 feeling wildly accomplished. Straight to the sweatpants.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun in a coat and scarf on a front porch at dusk holding a flashlight and looking up at the darkening sky. Text in the speech bubble reads: One: I used to be young, wild, and totally carefree. Now I catch myself saying, “I should probably head out before it gets dark.”

posts.quote: That moment you get into your pajamas, ready for bed, and realize it’s only 6:30. The end of daylight saving time is no joke.
posts.caption: The pajamas were on by 6:10. I'd had dinner, wiped the counter, and was feeling pretty good about the whole evening. Then I looked at the clock and it said 6:30, and the sky outside looked like midnight at the very least. Nothing in my body believes it's early. It would like the lamp off and the day closed. So I'm in the flannel with a long evening and a glass of something, and I've decided to be gracious about it. I'll watch a show. Then I'll watch the same show again.
posts.first: Last year I tried to stay up until nine just to prove I could. I got to 8:15, then spent forty minutes reading the same page. The book is still on the nightstand, bookmarked and a little embarrassed. We both know how it went.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun on a couch in flannel pajamas with a blanket over her knees, wide awake, a wall clock above her and a dark evening sky in the window. Text in the speech bubble reads: That moment you get into your pajamas, ready for bed, and realize it’s only 6:30. The end of daylight saving time is no joke.

posts.quote: Stray cats didn’t choose to be homeless. They’re just trying to get by. If you can’t help them, at least don’t hurt them.
posts.caption: There are two of them now, a grey one with a torn ear and a small orange one who waits on the step like she has an appointment. They showed up in September and I told myself I wouldn't. I put a bowl on the porch rail, and now there's a second bowl and a folded towel in the corner of a box. Nobody has named them yet, but I think they've named me. I'm the one who comes out at 6:30 with the can opener. It's a small job, and I like it.
posts.first: The orange one let me put a hand near her this week, not on her, just near. I counted that as a whole conversation. I'm moving the towel to the dry side of the porch before the rain this weekend. It seems like the polite thing to do.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of an older woman with silver-white hair and lavender glasses on a back porch putting down a bowl of food for two stray cats, a grey one and a small orange one. Text in the speech bubble reads: Stray cats didn’t choose to be homeless. They’re just trying to get by. If you can’t help them, at least don’t hurt them.

posts.quote: At this point in life my filter is pretty much gone. I’ve outlived most of the people who told me to watch my mouth, I survived the wild ’70s and ’80s, and I’ve handled enough real problems to know a few hurt feelings won’t end the world.
posts.caption: It left around 2009 and didn't send a forwarding address. I've learned to live with the quiet it left behind, such as it is.
posts.first: At a family dinner last month I said exactly what I thought about the casserole, and the room went silent for a full ten seconds. Then my cousin said thank you, somebody finally did. The casserole is still being served, which tells you something about everybody.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun standing with her hands on her hips and a calm smirk in a living room, a wine glass in one hand. Text in the speech bubble reads: At this point in life my filter is pretty much gone. I’ve outlived most of the people who told me to watch my mouth, I survived the wild ’70s and ’80s, and I’ve handled enough real problems to know a few hurt feelings won’t end the world.

posts.quote: I put on a podcast to fall asleep and now I know more about medieval shipbuilding than anyone should.
posts.caption: It was supposed to be a gentle voice and a slow story. Forty minutes in I was sitting up asking the ceiling about planking techniques. I now know a ship was built with the hull first, or maybe the frame first, depending on the century and who's arguing. I did not sleep. The narrator sounded very calm. I did learn that a particular kind of oak was reserved for the keel and everyone fought about it. Somehow I remember that better than my own dentist appointment. The ceiling lamp was on until 2:30, which I'd like on the record.
posts.first: I tried a different one the next night, about gardening. It was just as interesting and I stayed up learning about compost. The ceiling doesn't say much, but I think it's learning too. The ship was finished, I think. I never learned how it ended.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun lying awake in bed at night with one earbud in and a glowing phone on her chest, a wine glass and library books on the nightstand. Text in the speech bubble reads: I put on a podcast to fall asleep and now I know more about medieval shipbuilding than anyone should.

posts.template: F painted night scene (inbox image recreation)
posts.quote: That moment when you get your pajamas on and are ready for bed - only to realize it’s just 6:30. The daylight saving time struggle is real.
posts.caption: The sun had set by 4:50, which I didn't love, but the moon showed up early and looked great. It came up over the lake like it had been told to hurry, big and orange and unbothered. I stood at the back window in my slippers holding a mug I'd forgotten to drink from. Everyone on the street had already turned their lights on. The whole neighborhood seemed to have agreed to start the evening at once. I stayed at the window a little longer than the moon probably needed me to.
posts.first: I watched it rise for about twelve minutes and then got distracted by a squirrel on the fence. The squirrel was less interesting than the moon but more active. I went back to the moon. It was still there, which is more than I can say for most of my evening plans.
posts.alt: Painted illustration of a huge orange full moon over a dark calm lake, with a small woman in flannel pajamas holding a mug seen from behind at a window. Text in the night sky reads: That moment when you get your pajamas on and are ready for bed - only to realize it's just 6:30. The daylight saving time struggle is real.

posts.quote: All I want is to live in a world where I don’t mutter “What on earth is wrong with people?” every single time I leave the house.
posts.caption: I made it as far as the parking lot before the first one. That's an improvement on last week.
posts.first: I went to the grocery store on Saturday with a fixed plan to say nothing. I made it from the cart corral to the bread aisle. Someone had left a cart across the whole lane, and I said it out loud, to no one. The bread was fine.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun pushing a shopping cart down an empty supermarket aisle with a deadpan stare, a wine glass in her other hand and an abandoned cart ahead. Text in the speech bubble reads: All I want is to live in a world where I don’t mutter “What on earth is wrong with people?” every single time I leave the house.
